new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive and predictable. In non-verbal words primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable (monosyllables stressed; e.g. [ˈdamlu] 'nose', [ʔiˈmbali] 'thorn', [ˌlapaˈŋɡani] 'airstrip'); nominal enclitics are outside the stress domain. In inflected verbs primary stress is fixed on the verb stem (its only syllable, or the penult of a polysyllabic stem, ignoring a stem-final consonant), so long suffix strings do not shift it; prefixes, TAM suffixes and the dependency marker -mbo are never stressed; each stem in a serial verb construction takes its own primary stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Four-syllable (and the one five-syllable) words: secondary stress on the first syllable ([ˌlapaˈŋɡani], [ˌʔanjapaˈluku]). In verbs, secondary stresses fall on alternate syllables following the stem, skipping suffixes after the cross-reference suffixes (TAM, -mbo) which cannot be stressed.
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllabic grammatical words/clitics stressed only under emphasis; nominal clitics unstressed; verb prefixes and post-cross-reference suffixes unstressed; when vowel deletion removes the stressed vowel, stress goes to the conditioning vowel (2-230 [ˈfexo̯a]); negative semi-realis particle ga takes its own stress; syllables immediately before a serialised verb stem cannot bear secondary stress. Phonetic cue is intensity; in connected speech clausal intonation tracks word boundaries so stressed syllables need not be pitch-prominent; only /a/ reduces (mid-centralises) when unstressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress, illustrated on citation forms with phonetic transcriptions; clitics excluded from the domain; verbs computed on the stem (morphologically anchored) rather than the whole inflected word. Sec. 2.4.2 (p.118ff) treats word pitch/clausal intonation separately (H pitch on stressed syllables in isolation; boundary-marking M-H patterns in clauses).
new_statements.identity_note: The thesis describes Menggwa Dla (villages Menggwal, Wanggurinda, Wahai/Wamena area, PNG side and adjacent Indonesian villages), which de Sousa treats as one of two dialects of the Dla (= Dera, ISO kbv, dera1245) language, the other being 'Dla proper' spoken further west around Kamberatoro. Glottolog dera1245 has no dialect-level children, so the statement attaches to dera1245 with the note that it is based on the Menggwa dialect; WALS lists it as 'Dla (Menggwa)' code dlm with the same source.

sources.note: Stress predictable, not contrastive ('Words are not differentiated by suprasegmental features'); realised as intensity (+ higher pitch in isolation). Nouns/other words: monosyllables stressed; di- and trisyllables penultimate primary stress; 4-syllable words add secondary stress on the first syllable; nominal clitics unstressed. Verbs: primary stress on the verb stem (penult of polysyllabic stem, final C disregarded), secondary on alternate syllables after the stem, TAM/dependency suffixes and prefixes unstressed; each stem in a serial verb gets its own primary stress.
